paragraphs: Aquilas the convert (see above, Onkelos). He translated the Torah before R' Eliezer and R' Yehoshua, as found in Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 1:9:5 [Heilprin: halakhah 11]. They praised him, saying, ‘You are fairer than the sons of men.’ According to Me'or Einayim, chapter 45, he translated into Greek. That work established by proofs that Onkelos and Aquilas were both righteous converts and lived at one time, yet were not one person with two names: Onkelos the convert was an earlier associate, whereas Aquilas was a new student of R' Eliezer and R' Yehoshua. For Onkelos converted in Hillel's days and lived in the days of Rabban Gamliel the Elder, while Aquilas converted long after the destruction. In Shemot Rabbah, Mishpatim 30:12, Aquilas tells Emperor Andrinus that he wishes to convert. A parallel appears in the Buber Tanhuma, Mishpatim 3. In Bereshit Rabbah, chapter 70, Vayetze, on ‘Jacob vowed,’ Yefeh To'ar, section 5, writes that Aquilas was Andrinus's brother's son; Heilprin’s account says that Andrinus destroyed Betar more than fifty-two years after the destruction [de Rossi gives fifty-two years]. They call him Aquila, and he converted; one is called ‘Aquila Israel Mimer’ [wording retained]. Here ends the quotation from Me'or Einayim. In Shalshelet Ha-Kabbalah, folio 28a: Aquilas came to the Land of Israel to convert [Shalshelet reads לא״י; Heilprin prints לח״י] (this is in Bereshit Rabbah, Vayetze, chapter 70, and Midrash Kohelet, at the end of the passage ‘Better is the end of a thing’). He questioned R' Eliezer and found him irascible like Beit Shammai; he came to R' Yehoshua and found him humble like Hillel. He converted thirty-one years after the destruction, which was 104 of the Christian reckoning (this does not agree: since their reckoning begins in 3761, their year 104 is 3865, whereas thirty-one years after the destruction is 3859; it should read thirty-seven years after the destruction), and in Andrianus's fourth year. He converted on the island of Ponto and rendered the Torah from Hebrew into Greek. Torat Kohanim, Behar, likewise mentions Aquilas in Ponto. End quotation. This is in Torat Kohanim, Behar, chapter 1, section 9: ‘Not as Aquilas brought out his slaves—Pandos.’ Korban Aharon explains that Pandos was a place in Syria and Aquilas had slaves there. Also Vayikra Rabbah 11:9. In Midrash Hazit, on ‘For the fragrance of your oils,’ ‘among maidens’ is translated by Aquilas as ‘athnisia.’ Yefeh To'ar on Shemini there explains that he was from the city Athens. In Musaf He-Arukh, entry אפקלטורין, the wording is: At the beginning of Midrash Eikhah, ‘I clothed you in embroidered work’ is translated by Onkelos as ‘apeklatorin.’ In Midrash Hazit on ‘A locked garden,’ the reading is ‘Aquilas's translation: aplikta.’ It seems to me that one should read ‘Aquilas's translation,’ because he translated all Scripture into Greek, whereas Onkelos translated into Babylonian—unless Onkelos and Aquilas were one man who made two translations, one Babylonian and one Greek. End quotation.

In Vayikra Rabbah 11:9, on the verse at the end of Psalm 48, ‘Set your heart upon its rampart,’ etc., ‘He will lead us al mut,’ Aquilas's translation is ‘a world in which there is no death.’ The Arukh explains—and Mattenot Kehunah also brings this—that in Greek ‘thansia’ means death; following it they explain, ‘a world in which there is no death.’ In Sefer Ha-Ma'arikh: without an aleph at its beginning it signifies death. In Ma'arikh Ha-Ma'arakhah it is written that there is a kind of compound medicine called ‘athansia,’ which saves from deadly poison and is known to physicians. Yefeh To'ar on the aforementioned chapter writes as follows: ‘Athnisia: I wonder at the author of the Arukh, who wrote that thansia in Greek is death. What compelled him to this? Rather, clearly he was from a city named Athens, as we find in Eikhah Rabbati, in the passage “Great among the nations,” “one man from Athens”; it is mentioned there several times.’ End quotation. To my humble self, with a thousand requests for pardon, it seems clear that the Arukh's words are clearer than all the aforementioned commentators; far be it from a holy mouth to explain that it means he was from Athens. For this midrash occurs in four places: Jerusalem Talmud, Mo'ed Katan 3:7, ‘Aquilas's translation: athnasira, a world in which there is no,’ etc.; Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 2:4:5 [Heilprin: 2:3], ‘Aquilas's translation: athansitha, a world,’ etc.; and Midrash Hazit, on ‘For the fragrance of your oils,’ ‘Aquilas's translation: athansia, a world,’ etc. According to Yefeh To'ar, then, in all four places it must mean that Aquilas was from Athens. Yet in Bereshit Rabbah, Lekh Lekha 46:3, ‘I am El Shaddai,’ Aquilas's translation is ‘absios and ankos’; Yedei Moshe explains in the name of Me'or Einayim that this is Greek for ‘imperishable.’ In Vayetze, chapter 70, he is mentioned thus: ‘Aquilas the convert asked R' Eliezer.’ In Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 1:9:5, in Heilprin’s compressed citation, R' Hiyya bar Abba said [the Yerushalmi has R' Yirmeyah in his name]: ‘Aquilas the convert translated the Torah before R' Eliezer and R' Yehoshua, and they praised him, saying, “You are fairer than the sons of men.”’ In Midrash Hazit, on ‘A locked garden,’ ‘I clothed you in embroidered work’ has Aquilas's translation ‘aplikta.’ In Jerusalem Talmud Kiddushin 1:1:32, Aquilas the convert translated before R' Akiva ‘and she is a slave-woman neherefet’ as ‘crushed,’ as in ‘You pound groats upon him.’ In Esther Rabbah, on ‘White linen, karpas, and blue,’ Aquilas translated ‘airinon karpasinon.’ Thus nowhere does it mention that he was from Athens [אתנם in this occurrence], except in the four aforementioned places on ‘al mut—athansia, a world in which there is no death.’ Moreover, in all the places it gives the word's Greek translation: El Shaddai—absios; embroidered work—aplikta; harufah—like groats. Here, however, according to Yefeh To'ar, it would not explain the word al mut in Greek, because he takes athansia to mean ‘from Athens.’ Rather, it is clear and true that athansia is Greek, explaining ‘He will lead us al mut’ as ‘a world in which there is no death.’ Furthermore, Me'or Einayim, chapter 45, says Aquilas the convert translated the Torah into Greek. Shalshelet Ha-Kabbalah, folio 28, says he converted on the island of Ponto; Torat Kohanim, Behar, likewise says Aquilas had slaves in Ponto. In Musaf He-Arukh, entry פנטוס: ‘In the land of Shinar’ (Genesis 10) is rendered in the Jerusalem Targum as Pontus; it is a district in Asia, and Aquilas the convert came from there. End quotation. See what I wrote in Part I, year 3884. The truth thus bears witness to itself. Whoever wrote ‘perhaps they are one man’ did not see what I wrote above. Musaf He-Arukh writes, entry פנטוס: ‘In the land of Shinar’ is translated ‘in the land of Pontus’; it is a district in Asia, from which Aquilas the convert came. See above, Part I, year 3884: he was a priest and became a righteous convert. In Bereshit Rabbah, chapters 69 and 70, and Midrash Kohelet on ‘Better is the end of a thing,’ he questioned R' Yehoshua. See Yefeh To'ar at the beginning of Vayigash: Aquilas is not Onkelos.
